This publication is part of WHO's recommendations on non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections. It is made publicly available for transparency and informational purposes, as required by WHO guidelines. The recommendations are based on evidence graded using the GRADE system, which assesses the certainty of evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low, depending on the likelihood that the effect will differ substantially from the research findings. High-certainty evidence indicates a very low likelihood of substantial differences in effect, while moderate-certainty evidence suggests a moderate likelihood. Low-certainty evidence indicates a high likelihood of substantial differences, and very low-certainty evidence provides unreliable indications of the likely effect. Substantial differences refer to changes significant enough to influence decision-making. The publication includes references to various studies and trials that evaluate interventions aimed at reducing unnecessary cesarean sections. These include randomized controlled trials, cluster-randomized trials, and other methodologies. The studies assess interventions such as education programs, decision aids, psychosocial support, and policy changes, among others. The outcomes measured include cesarean section rates, maternal and neonatal health, and patient satisfaction. The publication also discusses methodological considerations, such as downgrading evidence due to risks of bias, imprecision, or confounding factors. For example, changes in cesarean section rates are analyzed using interrupted time-series methods, which assess changes in level and trend before and after interventions. Negative changes in level and slope indicate reductions in cesarean section rates. The references cited include studies from various countries and contexts, highlighting the global effort to address unnecessary cesarean sections through evidence-based, non-clinical interventions.
